_readme: THE TOPPS POKEMON RELEASES, WRITTEN BY A HUMAN, WITH A CITATION ON EVERY
FACT. Read by scripts/build-topps.mjs. Nothing here comes from a price feed
and nothing here may be guessed.
WHY THIS FILE EXISTS AT ALL. data/topps-top.json is written from
PriceCharting's crawl and knows exactly one thing: what a product record is
worth. It does not know what year Topps shipped a set, how many cards were
in it, or which film a movie set is about. Those are facts about a print run
from 1999 to 2004 and a price guide is not a source for them. So they live
here, each with the url they were read from, and /topps.html prints nothing
in this shape that this file does not carry.
THE TWO TAXONOMIES DO NOT LINE UP, AND THAT IS THE MOST IMPORTANT THING IN
THIS FILE. Topps shipped TWELVE sets, eleven in the States and one in
Europe only. PriceCharting files THIRTY-THREE
'consoles' under names like '2000 Topps TV Die Cut', and those are card TYPE
buckets, not Topps releases: a set's die-cut chase cards are split off into
their own bucket, and two Topps sets that shared a card type are merged into
one. '2000 Topps TV Heroes & Villians' holds HV1 to HV17, which is Series
2's five Heroes & Villains cards AND Series 3's twelve, in one bucket that
was never a Topps product. A page that prints PriceCharting's set names as
if they were Topps' set names is telling a reader that Topps released a set
called Heroes & Villains. It did not.
SO EVERY `pcConsoles` ENTRY BELOW IS A CLAIM AND MOST OF THEM CARRY THEIR
EVIDENCE. An `expect` block is a shape our own cached crawl must have if
the mapping is right, and it was written by comparing that shape against
the count Bulbapedia states for the subset: 19 OR-prefixed numbers where
Bulbapedia says series 3 had 19 Orange Islands episode cards, 62 numbers
running 152 to 249 where it says Johto series 1 had 62 Pokemon cards. Run
`node scripts/build-topps.mjs` and it recomputes every one of them from
data/topps-top.json and FAILS THE BUILD on a mismatch, so the mapping is
checked on every build rather than asserted once and left. An entry with no
`expect` is one where the two counts did not line up exactly; those are
mapped on the bucket name alone and the page does not print a count for
them. See that script's header.
WHAT IS DELIBERATELY ABSENT. No pull rates and no pack odds, for Topps or
anything else, which is a hard site rule. Bulbapedia states insert odds for
some of these sets; they were read and not recorded, and they must not be
added here later. No print-run totals, because no source we could reach
publishes one. No card stock or thickness comparison against Pokemon TCG
cards, because nothing sourceable says one. And no licensing counterparty:
who Topps signed the Pokemon licence with is not stated by any source we
could reach, so the page says the licence existed and does not name the
other side of it.

bulbapedia.name: Bulbapedia
bulbapedia.note: The Topps hub page and one page per set. Used for every set name, date and card count below.

pricecharting.name: PriceCharting
pricecharting.note: Prices and card scans only. Never used for a date, a name or a card count.

window.why: First Topps Pokemon set August 1999, last June 2004.

notTcg.quote: Topps does not manufacture any cards for use with the official Pokémon Trading Card Game.
note: This is the load-bearing fact on the whole page and it is a direct quote
rather than a summary, because everything else about what these cards are
follows from it. What does NOT follow, and is written as a consequence
rather than as a sourced fact: that a Topps card carries no HP, no
attacks, no energy cost, no weakness, no resistance and no retreat cost.
No source we reached spells that list out. The page states it as what
follows from a card not being made for the game, which is what it is.

neverReleased.name: Pokemon Top 10 Collector Cards
neverReleased.what: A Topps set planned for Pokemon's 10th anniversary in 2006 and never released. It is not part of the run above and is easy to meet in a checklist and mistake for one.

printings.what: A silver foil parallel of a base card. Series 1 printed a silver foil and a rainbow foil version of all 90 of its cards alongside the plain one.
The second foil parallel, with a chromatic shine across it rather than a flat silver one.
Sparkle-Chrome, one of the three insert parallels sitting above a plain Chrome card. Chrome Series 1 and 2 both printed every number in Chrome, Spectra-Chrome, Sparkle-Chrome and Tekno-Chrome.
Spectra-Chrome, the second of the three Chrome insert parallels.
Tekno-Chrome, the third Chrome insert parallel and the hardest of the four Chrome finishes to find. It is the finish on the most expensive raw Topps card in this whole ranking.
printings.scarcityQuote: The Jigglypuff card in question is of the Tekno rarity, making it one of the least common cards in the Topps Chrome Series 1 set.

printings.what: A hologram parallel or a hologram chase card, depending on the set.
PriceCharting's own label on eleven rows across the 1999 and 2000 TV sets. We could not source what Topps itself called them, so this guide says what the label is attached to and no more.

types.name: Chrome
types.what: A separate line of sets rather than an insert. Chrome cards are printed on chromium stock, are heavily embossed and very thick, and carry the Topps Chrome logo on the front and the back. The artwork matches the regular Trading Cards series.

types.name: Die cut
types.what: Chase cards cut to the shape of the Pokemon rather than to a rectangle, with raised embossing. Most Topps sets printed a run of them.

types.name: Evolution
types.what: Cards showing a Pokemon's evolutionary line. In the First Movie set the 12 Evolution cards are part of the base set and there are 12 die cut embossed versions of them as chase; in Advanced the 18 embossed Evolution cards cover six three-stage lines.

types.name: Sticker
types.what: Cards carrying a peelable Pokemon sticker, with puzzle pieces printed on the back that assemble into one image across the run.

types.name: Puzzle
types.what: Cards whose backs carry pieces of a picture. Series 1 put them on the backs of its 13 character cards, completing an image on the checklist card; series 3 printed 6 puzzle cards of their own.

types.name: Heroes & Villains
types.what: Character cards for the people in the anime rather than the Pokemon, describing who they are and what they want. They were part of the base set in series 2, series 3 and the Europe-only Johto Series 3. Topps never released a set called Heroes & Villains.

types.name: Pop-up
types.what: Cards with a punch-out Pokemon that props up off the card face.

types.name: Clear
types.what: Transparent cards with an image printed on both sides. Series 2 and series 3 printed five each.

types.name: First Appearance hologram
types.what: Six hologram cards in the Movie 2000 set for Pokemon making their first screen appearance in that film.

types.name: Authentic Film Frame
types.what: A card carrying a real 35mm frame cut from a print of the film. Topps said a full reel was cut into individual frames, one to a card, so no two of these cards hold the same frame.

tells.tell: The back is a Pokedex entry or an episode summary, not game text
tells.detail: A Topps card back carries a description of the Pokemon or a summary of the episode the picture is from. A Pokemon TCG card back is the blue Poke Ball pattern, identical on every card in the game.

tells.tell: The Topps logo is on the back, under the Pokedex entry
tells.detail: Card number at the top, Topps logo under the entry, copyright along the bottom. There is a Nintendo seal on the back too, circular on the UK first printing and oval on the North American one.

tells.tell: The picture is a still from the show or the film
tells.detail: Topps printed screen images. A Pokemon TCG card carries commissioned illustration with an artist credit on it.

tells.tell: There is no HP, no attack, no energy cost and no retreat cost
tells.detail: This one follows from the card not being made for the game rather than being quoted from a source, and it is the fastest check there is: turn the card over, and if there is nothing to play with, it is not a Pokemon TCG card.

tells.tell: On Series 1, the colour of the Topps logo dates the printing
tells.detail: Blue on the first printing, black on the second, green on the third and red on the fourth, the last two on non-foil cards only. The foil debossing changes with it: smooth on the first, then rays, then flames, then Poke Balls.

tells.tell: A Chrome card feels wrong in the hand before you look at it
tells.detail: Heavily embossed, noticeably thick, with the Topps Chrome logo on both faces. The glossy coating also makes them stick to each other.

notATell.detail: Measuring the card is the first thing people try and this guide cannot back it up. We found no source stating a size or a card stock difference between a Topps Pokemon card and a Pokemon TCG card, so no check here rests on one. Turn the card over instead: the back settles it in a second and every tell above is on that side.
